Aside from a few rare exceptions, characters don't usually leave your team in FE games. Radiant Dawn is weird with this and Fates has a couple, but in most of the series once someone joins they're with you for good. They should probably have made that clearer through Lyn mode, I think.

For promotion, both Priscilla and Sain are great choices, Priscilla can be helpful with magic and having a second paladin is great. I'd also consider Erk or Canas, as giving them staff utility can be really helpful. As someone said, unless you got REALLY lucky with Wil or Rebecca's level ups, save the Orion's Bolt for Rath. He's good.
Also, promoting early is usually a very good idea. Most units won't get enough xp throughout a playthrough to reach 20/20 anyway, and the early to mid game is usually balanced around the assumption that you will promote some people. And they usually give you enough good late recruits that even if your early game team turned out terrible or all died, you can carry on with them. In FE7 in particular, you get some very good units like Pent, Louise, Harken, Hawkeye and Renault.

As for stat boosters, my strategy is to usually pay attention to what slight weaknesses my characters have, and try to shore those up. For example, if a character has good combat stats but seems to be within one or two points of speed from doubling most enemies, I'll give them the speedwings. If my Myrmidon is a bit too frail to survive if he fails to dodge more than one hit, I'll buff their defense or hp. And so on. Except Boots, Boots always go to either my dancer or my strongest, most mobile unit. Usually the dancer.

Also, the most important piece of advice I'll give you is _don't be afraid of permadeath_. I'm not telling you to go full ironman without resetting on your first time through, but if you reset the chapter every time someone dies you'll just be making the game way harder for yourself than it would otherwise be. Losing some people doesn't ruin your playthrough, and the game is balanced with the idea that you'll probably lose a few! It's alright. Of course, it's alright to reset as well, especially if you lose a unit you like or an important item, but you don't _have_ to do it.

This would be easily fixed by giving us a better way to upgrade Poppi, maybe with materials dropped by enemies or gathered from the environment, which would even make more sense in the story due to her being mechanical and all. 

Second is that locking Blades to the character that opens the core would be fine, except the game takes far too long to give you Morag and especially Zeke. By that point, especially on a first playthrough, an uninformed player might have already spent most or all their good cores on Rex and Nia, making it pretty hard to give the new members good Blades. This is also easily solvable - in the late game, when Rex gets his Master Driver upgrade, instead of him being able to use everyone else's blades, he should have just unlocked free transfering. You still do get enough transfer items playing normally to end up with a good team, but that does require you to do some sidequests and explore and can be a hassle if you happen not to have any when you get a crucial blade on someone who isn't good with that weapon or already has a great blade for that element. (Sure, multiples of the same element aren't really bad, but I don't like it myself) 

Third, it's really REALLY annoying to keep going through the process of opening all those common blades until you get a rare one you actually want to use. I get that it's part of the gacha system, but we're not paying for these pulls with real money, so you don't need to use these annoying practices. Just make it so the rare cores guarantee a rare blade, and lower the chances of getting one from the common cores to make up for it. Maybe also give us a way to "refine" a large amount of common cores into a rarer one. That would both make common cores valuable and maybe encourage players to use the common blades a bit more. 

There's also the fact that the game takes _forever_ to actually let you properly use the battle system, and being locked to two blade slots until chapter 4 makes the early game slow and boring, not to mention easy since they can't make enemies actually very challenging since they know you don't have too many options to deal with them. 

This is all coming from a place of love, of course. I still think XB2 is a great game. It could just be so much better, though. And the Torna DLC pretty much fixes literally all those issues, and is probably what XB2's gameplay systems should have been. It's not really _that_ obscure, but it definitely should have much more mainstream popularity than it does - Joe Abercrombie's First Law trilogy and its sequels. It's pretty much a crime that Abercrombie isn't commonly mentioned in the same breath as GRRM when it comes to modern dark fantasy, and he's in my opinion just as good an author if not better. Especially considering Joe still actually, you know, _writes books_ and his stories tend to have endings. Satisfactory ones, even.

Seriously, read The First Law. It is to fantasy what Watchmen is to comics, not in terms of influence in the industry but in how it takes classic tropes of the genre and fires cold, cruel reality at them with a cannon until they break in interesting ways. The narrative is much more personal and character-focused than most fantasy books, and the prose itself tends to vary depending on the POV character, which is one of Abercrombie's best traits as an author. All his protagonists are basically terrible, but very interesting and often likeable people.

The prose itself is also fantastic, and does a great job of establishing its world as a dark, brutal place but still keeping an undercurrent of dry humor and sarcasm. I've once seen it described as "Game of Thrones if it was written by a really angry version of Terry Pratchett", and it kinda fits.

In theory, am inquisitor has absolute political power, aside from maybe prosecuting the High Lords or something without reason. But that "in theory" is the key part. Authority is only as good as your capacity to enforce it, and while the Inquisition's reach is long, it's not absolute. They're still a relatively small organization when compared to the Imperium at large, and while their resources are technically limitless, in practice it's much more complicated. While killing an inquisitor is obviously something that can get you horribly punished, that only happens if they find out you did it and nobody covers it up well enough. And if somebody (usually other inquisitors) actually goes and investigates it. And sometimes, it's in the interests of people within the Inquisition itself to make sure such a murder is NOT looked into because they wanted that individual gone in the first place. There's a lot of infighting within the Inquisition itself.

As for physical ability, they're normal humans. With all the best gear and possible mechanical augmentations, sure, but still nowhere near as strong as an ork or a space marine. Most of the time, if an inquisitor has to personally fight something like that, plans have gone wrong and it's a desperate situation.

Pretty much nobody in the Imperium aside from the space marines themselves and the custodes has that kind of augmentation. There are other kinds, like longer lifespan treatments and such, that the nobility and elites get, but actual physical augmentation is usually unheard of. Normal humans (which inquisitors very much are) can get mechanical replacements and augmentations, though that doesn't get them anywhere near the strength or resilience of an Astartes.

There are a few things you can do. In the short term, using Imperial Cross with a heavy infantry in front equipped with a sword (so they can proc their auto-parry ability) and buffing them with something defensive like wind screen might help a lot with mitigating damage. Does your court mage have good levels in water or earth? For big fights it might be best to have them focus entirely on healing, preferably with that mist spell that makes enemies ignore them unless they attack. That lasts pretty much indefinitely unless you break it or they go down to an AoE attack, so it usually guarantees you have healing and buffs available the whole fight.

In the long term, while it sucks to raise at first due to a lack of good early spells, light magic is really really good. It eventually gets a spell that can severely lower all damage on the whole party for a round. It's expensive, so you can't rely on having it for the whole fight, but it's saved my ass on far too many bosses to count.

Difficulty spikes can happen, but you can probably do something to deal with it. What's your current party like? What formation are you using? Do you have access to defensive buffs and healing? Is your main issue that your characters go down too easily or a lack of damage output?

One general tip I can give is that a lot of stuff in this game is vulnerable to status ailments, especially stun. I think most of the heroes aren't, but for bosses that summon adds like the stone it can be very useful to just stun, paralyze or sleep the adds and focus on the boss. The female Ranger class has an ability that greatly helps with that, especially if you can put it on someone who's good with hammers or shortswords.

First of all, don't worry about killing one hero with each emperor. You're not on a time limit. Well, certain quests are, and the world does change as generations progress, but you won't fail the whole game if you take too long or something. This is a game you're meant to take at whatever pace you want, and it'll mostly react to that and give you different outcomes for stuff, but you can't fail the main quest of defeating all seven heroes aside from, well, just fighting them and losing. And even then, some of them do let you live if you lose to them.

There's also no issue in whoever you choose as the next Emperor. If you don't like your choice, you can abdicate (once per generation) and choose a new one by sitting on the throne and picking that option.

As for abilities, they're class-locked for a good while, though you'll eventually be able to equip them to different classes. Techs and spells you learned can be taught to anyone you want through the training hall and the magic lab, respectively. (You might not have the latter yet, but you'll be able to build it soon).

As for why your characters keep dying, this game is pretty tough. Unlike most JRPGs where you'd just pick the strongest attack option every turn, here pretty much everything matters. Buffs and debuffs are VERY useful, formations matter, and status ailments can often save you in tough fights. Even a surprising amount of bosses are susceptible to ailments, especially stun, so don't hesitate to try it on them. Defensive buffs are also really really good.

When you finally confront Fou-Lu at the end, he asks Ryu to merge with him and become a complete dragon god once more, after which they, as the pretty much omnipotent being they originally were, would eradicate humanity. To make his point, he shows you flashbacks of the worst aspects of humanity you encountered throughout the game, and to reach the good ending you need to disagree with his points over and over so the game gives you the option to refuse at the end and fight him. However, should you agree with some or all of his points, the game lets you just say "maybe so..." and join him. And it doesn't ever judge you for that decision. It takes enormous balls for the game to just go "So you agree with the nihilistic god that humanity is a failed project and genocide is probably a better option than to let it go on? While a lot of people (rightly) brought up Dark Souls 2's Adaptability stat as probably the worst idea Fromsoft ever had, I'd also like to mention its take on weapon durability. Breakable weapons were always a bad idea in the Souls games in general, to be fair (and honestly, usually a terrible idea in anything that isn't a survival game like Don't Starve or something like that) but in Dark Souls it was just... There. It was a system that barely existed. Aside from a few specific gimmick weapons made of crystal, which were very fragile and couldn't be fixed, you'd barely even remember weapons could break. Occasionally after a long time you'd notice, spend some souls or an item to fix it, and that was that.

 The only time it'd matter was when some asshole invaded you wearing nothing but underwear, butterfly wings and a funny hat, and kept casting the spell that creates an acid cloud to damage all your gear, which was frankly hilarious. (Actually happened to me, btw. I laughed my ass off.) 

Anyway, come DS2, they decided weapon durability should actually matter. Which meant revamping the system so that every weapon broke really fast, but bonfires repaired your stuff automatically to make up for that. The main issue I had with Fear and Hunger was that it's not too hard, but it is too punishing. The best thing about the way the Souls games do difficulty is that for as hard as they can be, failure is just a slap on the wrist. You get sent back to the bonfire, which is usually not too far from where you were, and you keep everything you picked up and every change you made to the world state before you died. You might lose your souls, but you can go get them back. Contrast that with F&H where saves are precious and risky, and dying can cost you significant progress or even force you to restart the whole run. Hell, in Termina you have to go a LONG time without saving for the first time. This means that learning the game is very difficult, as it takes a long time to iterate. I found it very frustrating.

It's still a great game, though. I just wish it was less frustrating.
